newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-Russia ride thrills keep investors coming.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Russia ride thrills keep investors coming.

text.p: A year of nail-biting uncertainty has left many foreign investors in Russia substantially better off. Analysts predict more will be tempted to try their luck there next year.
But the promise of less hair-raising politics and an economomy that is both stable and growing, mean the days of huge yields on Russian investments are largely over, they add.

It has been a year of major accomplishments and nerve-jarring uncertainty, ranging from the pledge of its largest ever loan by the International Monetary Fund to seeing a re-elected President Boris Yeltsin survive major heart surgery.
By last weeknd, the IMF had relased the delayed October tranche and the State Duma approved the 1997 budget draft on its first reading.
Many analysts believe Russia will start 1997 in its best economic and political shape since it emerged from a collapsed Soviet Union.
The list of obstacles and potential calamities remains long and one analyst warned of "Russia's great gift for producing nasty surprises," but the painful transition to market economics is working.
"The outlook for Russia is fundamentally good. The momentum of change is still there...but all the assets are going to remain volatile," ING Barings chief East Europe analyst Philip Poole said.
"It's difficult to say it's a screaming buy. I'm more bullish about Russia than a lot of the other emerging markets but the differentiation is not so extreme as it was,"
Treasury bills (GKOs), which were offering up 200 percent annual yields earlier this year, are now below 40 percent.
And the almost restructured Soviet commercial debt, which in 1996 has given its buyers up to 150 percent back on their investment, does not have room to rise much more.

"The worst is behind them. They've essentially cracked the problem of financial stability. It's now just a question of how quickly they can get the economy to grow," said senior Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel McGovern said.
Russia has managed to control inflation, bring down local interest rates, largely sorted out its foreign commercial debts and begun to tap international capital markets.

"The Russian economy has already fallen to half its original level. It's hard to see where it could decline further. 1997 will be a year of growth but don't ask me by how much," said one London-based international economist.
He also noted that about a third of the economy is outside the official data in the "shadow economy."

Vital issues remain of how to get the economy growing after steep falls in output since the end of the Soviet Union, secure a budget and make sure there is enough tax revenue to get the social spending up to more reasonable levels.
Apart from tax collection, Russia needs to get privatisation back on track, implement a more sound legal framework and deal with corruption, analysts said.

"Fiscal policy is the key," said Paribas East Europe analyst Stuart Brown. "The inadequacies of Russian fiscal policy pose a serious impendiment to growth and the greater stability that would come with less...inequality."
For Brown, tax compliance was less crucial than ineffective bankruptcy enforement and falling profit taxes.
ING's Poole and some others picked out Russian shares as the asset with the potential to mushroom next year.
"If there is a market that will take off in 1997, it is the Russian equity market," said Poole who suggested investors stick initially to the more liquid global depostiary receipts.
